title: Maternal and Child Health
summary: Learn how to keep mothers, newborns and young children healthy: antenatal care and danger signs, safe birth and postnatal care, essential newborn care, infant feeding and growth, immunisation and childhood illness, and family planning and key indicators.
audience: Health students, community health workers, nurses, parents and NGO staff

body.p: Maternal and child health aims to keep mothers, newborns and young children alive and healthy. Most maternal and newborn deaths are preventable with good care before, during and after birth.

WHO recommends at least eight antenatal care contacts during pregnancy, the first in the first 12 weeks. Visits check the mother's and baby's health, screen for problems such as anaemia, high blood pressure, HIV and syphilis, give tetanus vaccination, iron and folic acid supplements, and prepare for birth.

Pregnancy is counted from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP). A simple estimate of the due date adds 280 days (40 weeks): an LMP of 1 March 2026 gives an estimated due date of 6 December 2026. On 14 June 2026 the pregnancy would be 15 weeks. Ultrasound early in pregnancy dates it more accurately.

body.h: Danger signs in pregnancy needing urgent care

list: Vaginal bleeding.
Severe headache, blurred vision or fits (possible pre-eclampsia).
Severe abdominal pain.
Fever and feeling very unwell.
Reduced or absent baby movements later in pregnancy.
Leaking fluid before labour, or labour before 37 weeks.

body.tip: Help every pregnant woman make a birth plan: where she will give birth, how she will get there quickly, and who will support her.

body.p: Giving birth with a skilled birth attendant (midwife, nurse or doctor) in a facility able to manage complications greatly reduces deaths. Leading causes of maternal death include severe bleeding after birth, infections, high blood pressure disorders (pre-eclampsia and eclampsia), complications of unsafe abortion and obstructed labour.

list: Monitoring labour progress with a partograph or labour care guide.
Giving a uterotonic medicine (such as oxytocin) after birth to prevent heavy bleeding.
Clean hands, clean surfaces and clean cord cutting to prevent infection.
Recognising and referring complications quickly.

body.p: The first days and weeks are high-risk for mother and baby. Postnatal checks should happen within 24 hours and in the first week, checking bleeding, blood pressure, fever, breastfeeding, the mother's mood and the baby's health. Danger signs for the mother include heavy bleeding, fever, severe headache and difficulty breathing.

body.tip: Postnatal depression is common and treatable; ask new mothers how they are feeling, not just how the baby is.

body.p: The first hours of life are critical. Essential newborn care includes:

list: Drying the baby immediately and keeping it warm, ideally through skin-to-skin contact with the mother.
Starting breastfeeding within the first hour.
Clean cord care, keeping the cord dry.
Helping babies who do not breathe at birth (newborn resuscitation by trained staff).
Eye care, vitamin K and birth-dose vaccines according to national schedules.
Kangaroo mother care for small and preterm babies: continuous skin-to-skin contact and frequent breastfeeding, which saves lives.
Not feeding well or unable to suck.
Fits, or very sleepy and difficult to wake.
Fast breathing or chest in-drawing.
Fever or the baby feeling cold.
Yellow skin in the first day or on the palms and soles (jaundice).
Redness or pus around the cord.

body.tip: Teach families the newborn danger signs before they go home, and make sure they know where to go if they see one.

body.p: WHO and UNICEF recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months (no other food or water), then nutritious complementary foods with continued breastfeeding up to two years or beyond. Breast milk protects against infections and provides all the nutrients a young baby needs.

list: Start with soft, mashed foods and gradually increase thickness, amount and variety.
Include animal-source foods (eggs, fish, meat), legumes, vegetables and fruit; enrich porridges.
Feed responsively: watch for hunger and fullness cues.
Keep food and utensils clean, and wash hands before preparing food.

body.p: Regular weighing and length measurements plotted on growth charts (in the child's health card) show whether a child is growing well. Faltering growth is an early warning of illness or poor feeding. Stunting (low height for age) reflects long-term undernutrition; wasting (low weight for height) is acute and dangerous, and is screened for in communities using mid-upper-arm circumference tapes.

body.tip: Ask parents to bring the child's health card to every visit; it holds the growth chart and vaccination record.

body.p: Vaccination protects children against measles, polio, diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, tuberculosis, pneumococcal disease, rotavirus diarrhoea, hepatitis B and more. Follow the national immunisation schedule and catch up missed doses.

list: Pneumonia: fast breathing or chest in-drawing in a child with cough needs prompt assessment and treatment.
Diarrhoea: give oral rehydration solution (ORS) and zinc, continue feeding, and seek care for blood in the stool or signs of dehydration.
Malaria in endemic areas: test and treat fever promptly; children should sleep under insecticide-treated nets.
Malnutrition, which makes all other illnesses more deadly.

body.h: General danger signs (from the IMCI approach)

body.p: A child who is unable to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, has had convulsions, or is lethargic or unconscious needs urgent referral. Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guides health workers through assessing and treating sick children systematically.

body.tip: Hand washing with soap, safe water, breastfeeding and vaccination together prevent a large share of childhood deaths.

body.p: Family planning lets people choose whether and when to have children. Spacing births at least two years apart improves the health of mothers and babies. Methods include implants, injectables, intrauterine devices, pills, condoms (which also protect against sexually transmitted infections) and permanent methods. Counselling should be respectful, voluntary and informed.

list: Maternal mortality ratio: maternal deaths per 100 000 live births. 45 maternal deaths among 12 000 live births is 45 / 12 000 x 100 000 = 375.
Infant mortality rate: deaths before age one per 1000 live births. 540 infant deaths among 12 000 births is 45 per 1000.
Neonatal mortality: deaths in the first 28 days per 1000 live births.
Coverage indicators: antenatal visits, skilled birth attendance, immunisation and exclusive breastfeeding rates.

body.p: The Sustainable Development Goals aim to reduce the global maternal mortality ratio to below 70 per 100 000 live births and end preventable deaths of newborns and children under five by 2030.

body.tip: Community health workers are vital links: they find pregnant women early, promote healthy practices and refer danger signs quickly.
